Volume 02 - Frontend + Backend Foundations
Phase 06 - Next.js <-> NestJS Communication

This package contains 10 focused Phase 06 PDFs, one combined complete book, and a reference end-to-end TaskFlow snapshot.

Phase boundaries:
- Next.js and NestJS are now connected end to end.
- Server Component fetch and browser Client Component fetch are both taught.
- Browser CORS is configured intentionally for local frontend origins.
- JSON POST preflight behavior is demonstrated.
- Raw fetch remains visible; TanStack Query is intentionally later.
- Todo data remains in memory.
- No Prisma/PostgreSQL yet.
- No authentication/authorization yet.

Primary references:
- Next.js App Router Fetching Data / fetch documentation
- Next.js Environment Variables documentation
- NestJS CORS documentation
- MDN CORS, preflight and Fetch API documentation

product still has a missing link: the frontend has not consumed the backend contract. Phase 06 creates that link deliberately.

CORS is a browser security policy. A server-to-server fetch is not blocked by the browser CORS enforcement model.

Figure - Server Component fetch versus browser Client Component fetch. Knowing where code executes explains when CORS
becomes relevant.

In the App Router, a Server Component can await fetch directly. That request originates from the Next.js server process. A
Client Component runs JavaScript in the browser after hydration; its fetch originates from the browser. Both can target the
same NestJS URL, but the security and observability characteristics differ.

enforcement?

as direct API call?

Do not turn this into dogma

The course is not saying all reads must be server-side or all mutations must be client-side. The point is to understand the
execution environment first. Later architecture decisions can then be made intentionally.

The browser is not the Next.js server
This distinction becomes one of the most important full-stack debugging skills. If a server-side fetch fails, browser CORS
settings are irrelevant. If a browser-side fetch is blocked by CORS, changing Prisma or React rendering will not fix it.
Always identify where the failing code executed.

Book 2 of Phase 06

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 06                                                        API URLs and Environment Boundaries

URLs are configuration, not component content
During local development, Next.js listens on port 3000 and NestJS on port 4000. It is tempting to paste http://localhost:4000
into every component. That works for ten minutes and becomes painful as soon as staging or production exists. We introduce
the smallest useful configuration boundary now.

apps/web/.env.local
.env.local - local file, do not commit

API_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:4000
NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:4000

apps/web/.env.example
.env.example - safe contract, commit this

API_BASE_URL=
NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL=

Why two variables?
Variable                                Available where?                   Purpose

API_BASE_URL                            Server runtime only                Server Components and server-only code

NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL                Browser bundle + server            Browser/client code that must know the public API
URL

Next.js only exposes environment values to browser code when they are explicitly prefixed with NEXT_PUBLIC_. Those
public values are inlined into browser JavaScript at build time, so they must never contain secrets.

SECURITY BOUNDARY

A value being called an environment variable does not make it secret. NEXT_PUBLIC_* means the value is intentionally public
to the browser. API URLs are normally fine; database passwords and service-role keys are not.

Environment variable location
When a Next.js project uses a src/ directory, environment files still belong at the project root, such as apps/web/.env.local,
not inside apps/web/src.

Normalize one development hostname
Use either localhost consistently or 127.0.0.1 consistently while learning. Browsers treat origin as scheme + host + port.
http://localhost:3000 and http://127.0.0.1:3000 are different origins even though both reach the same machine. Our Nest
CORS example allows both to reduce accidental local friction, but consistency remains a good habit.

Fail early when required configuration is absent
Server-side example

const apiBaseUrl = process.env.API_BASE_URL;

if (!apiBaseUrl) {
throw new Error('API_BASE_URL is not configured');
}

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 06                                                             API URLs and Environment Boundaries

REAL-WORLD NOTE

Later deployments may use different internal and public API addresses. Keeping the server and browser configuration concepts
separate now prepares the architecture for that difference without adding deployment complexity yet.

Why GET may work while POST suddenly shows OPTIONS
A simple cross-origin GET can often proceed without an OPTIONS preflight. A browser POST that sends Content-Type:
application/json is different: application/json is not a CORS-safelisted content type, so the browser commonly checks
permission first.

Browser wants POST /todos
Content-Type: application/json

OPTIONS /todos
CORS preflight

NestJS CORS response
Access-Control-Allow-*

POST /todos
actual JSON request

201 Created
Todo representation

Figure - A JSON cross-origin POST commonly triggers an automatic browser preflight. The frontend normally does not hand-code the
OPTIONS request.

Create helper
Add to apps/web/src/lib/api/todos.ts

export async function createTodo(baseUrl: string, title: string): Promise<Todo> {
const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/todos`, {
method: 'POST',
headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
body: JSON.stringify({ title }),
});

if (!response.ok) {
throw new Error(`POST /todos failed: ${response.status}`);
}

return response.json() as Promise<Todo>;
}

The browser owns the preflight
The frontend normally does not write an OPTIONS request manually. The browser decides that a cross-origin request
requires preflight, sends OPTIONS with the intended method/headers, inspects the server CORS response, and only then
sends the actual request if policy allows it.

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 06                                                          CORS Preflight and Fetch Error Semantics

Network error vs HTTP error
Situation                     fetch promise                  Response available?              What to inspect

API process stopped           Rejects                        No                               catch / network error

DNS or malformed URL          Rejects                        No                               URL/configuration

CORS blocked browser          Typically rejects to JS as a   No usable response               Console + Network + CORS headers
access                        network-style failure

404 Not Found                 Resolves                       Yes, ok=false                    status + response body

500 Server Error              Resolves                       Yes, ok=false                    status + server logs

IMPORTANT FETCH RULE

A try/catch around fetch is not enough to detect HTTP failures. Check response.ok or response.status because 404 and 500 are
still valid HTTP responses.

Preflight debugging checklist
●     Was the browser request actually cross-origin?
●     Did the Network panel show OPTIONS before the actual method?
●     What Origin header did the browser send?
●     Did the API return Access-Control-Allow-Origin for that exact origin?
●     Did Access-Control-Allow-Methods include the intended method?
●     Did Access-Control-Allow-Headers permit non-safelisted headers?
●     Did the actual request run after OPTIONS?

Do not "fix" CORS with no-cors
Setting fetch mode to no-cors is not a general solution. It produces an opaque response whose useful status/body are not
available to application JavaScript. The correct fix is an intentional server CORS policy when the browser should be allowed
to call the API.

What belongs in lib/api/todos.ts

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 06                                                                       A Clean API Client Boundary

export interface Todo {
id: number;
title: string;
completed: boolean;
}

async function expectJson<T>(response: Response): Promise<T> {
if (!response.ok) {
throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status} for ${response.url}`);
}
return response.json() as Promise<T>;
}

export async function fetchTodos(baseUrl: string) {
return expectJson<Todo[]>(await fetch(`${baseUrl}/todos`, { cache: 'no-store' }));
}

export async function createTodo(baseUrl: string, title: string) {
return expectJson<Todo>(await fetch(`${baseUrl}/todos`, {
method: 'POST',
headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
body: JSON.stringify({ title }),
}));
}

Why pass baseUrl instead of reading process.env inside
the helper?
The same pure HTTP helper can run in a Server Component with API_BASE_URL and in a Client Component with
NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL. If the helper itself imported a server-only variable, it would become unsafe to reuse
from client code. Passing configuration makes the execution boundary explicit.

NOT A REPOSITORY YET

This module is a small transport helper. It does not pretend HTTP is interchangeable with memory/database implementations,
and it does not introduce interfaces merely for architecture style. Repository Pattern arrives only after the course has a concrete
reason for it.

Debug the path, not the symptom
"The page is blank" is not a diagnosis. End-to-end development becomes manageable when every failure is located on the
actual request path.

Is Next.js running?
port 3000

Is NestJS running?
port 4000

What exact URL did fetch use?
environment variable

Did the request leave the browser?
Network tab

Was there OPTIONS first?
preflight

What status + headers returned?
HTTP evidence

Did fetch code check response.ok?
application handling

Figure - Phase 06 debugging follows the network path instead of guessing from the UI symptom.

Browser Network panel workflow
1      Open DevTools -> Network.
2      Clear previous entries.
3      Trigger exactly one operation.
4      Select the request to port 4000.
5      Inspect Request URL and Request Method.
6      Inspect Status Code.
7      Inspect Request Headers, especially Origin and Content-Type.
8      Inspect Response Headers, especially Access-Control-Allow-* when cross-origin.
9      Inspect Response/Preview body.
10     If OPTIONS exists, inspect it separately from the actual request.

Terminal evidence still matters
A Server Component fetch runs in the Next.js server process, so its stack trace and fetch error appear in the Next.js terminal.
A NestJS handler failure appears in the API terminal. A browser Client Component failure can appear in browser
Console/Network. Good debugging follows the process that executed the failing code.

FULL_STACK_DEVELOPER_2026_COMPLETE - Phase 06                                                               DevTools and End-to-End Debugging

Failure matrix
Symptom                                               Likely layer to inspect first

Next /todos page throws when API is stopped           Next.js server fetch / API process

Browser says CORS policy blocked request              Browser + API CORS headers

GET returns 404                                       Exact method/path and Nest route

fetch catch runs with Failed to fetch                 Network/CORS rather than HTTP 4xx/5xx

response.ok is false with 500                         Nest logs / application failure

Public API URL changed but browser still uses old     NEXT_PUBLIC_ build-time inlining / restart-build context
value

Smallest-correction discipline

Do not change CORS, fetch, controllers, service logic and environment files simultaneously. Preserve one failing request, make
one hypothesis, change one layer, rerun the same request, then observe whether the evidence changed.

A powerful test: bypass the browser
If a browser call fails, repeat the equivalent request with PowerShell. If PowerShell succeeds while browser JavaScript fails,
that strongly narrows the problem toward browser-only policy/configuration such as CORS. It does not prove CORS
automatically, but it prevents pointless database or controller rewrites.

Debugging Workshop — Phase 06: Next.js <-> NestJS Communication

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
Next.js component/action -> API client -> HTTP request -> CORS/origin rules -> NestJS -> HTTP response -> UI state

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — Using the browser-only URL from server-to-server code in deployment
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 2 — Wildcard CORS with credentials

Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Do not hide the evidence
Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant.

Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Next.js <-> NestJS Communication

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 06 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Connect Next.js and NestJS through an explicit, debuggable HTTP boundary with environment-safe base URLs and correct CORS behavior.

Required artifact
A typed API client boundary that can call the NestJS health/tasks endpoints from the appropriate Next.js execution context.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can locate a failure on frontend, network, or API side.
• Can explain CORS as a browser policy.
• Can configure environment-specific API URLs.
• Can build one reusable request helper.

Independent build sequence
1. Define API base URLs per environment instead of hard-coding localhost throughout components.
2. Call a public endpoint from a Server Component and inspect where the request originates.
3. Call an endpoint from a Client Component and observe browser CORS behavior.
4. Configure NestJS CORS for the exact development origin and credentials policy required.
5. Centralize response parsing and non-2xx error handling in one API helper.
6. Use Network tab plus API logs to trace one failing request end-to-end.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.
